rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣarrafnā means repeatedly turning something from state to state; its understood object is the Quranic meaning, expressed and established through varied formulations.
rows.anchor: من التصريف وهو كثرة صرف الشيء من حال إلى حال ومفعوله هنا محذوف للعلم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran can mean the whole revelation, with the phrase locating this repeated treatment in its passages; alternatively it means passages refuting attribution of daughters to God.
rows.anchor: فالمراد بالقرآن مجموع التنزيل وجوز أن يراد به البعض المشتمل على إبطال إضافة البنات إليه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object may be the argument refuting that attribution; Quran may name the container for its meaning, or the verb may be treated as intransitive and governed by fī.
rows.anchor: أي صرفنا القول المشتمل على إبطال الإضافة المذكورة في هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A lighter reading of ṣarrafnā is also transmitted; it has the same basic meaning but lacks the intensive force of the doubled form.
rows.anchor: بالتخفيف والصرف كالتصريف إلا في التكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose is that people remember, take admonition, and become reassured, since repetition produces assent and tranquility.
rows.anchor: ليتذكروا ويتعظوا ويطمئنوا له فإن التكرار يقتضي الإذعان واطمئنان النفس

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read the verb here and in al-Furqān from dhikr, meaning recollection opposite forgetfulness and heedlessness; the other reading means taking admonition.
rows.anchor: من الذكر الذي هو بمعنى التذكر ضد النسيان والغفلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite this varied presentation, the disbelievers only become more averse from truth; the shift to third person signals that their conduct warrants turning away and recounting their misdeeds.
rows.anchor: عن الحق وإعراضا عنه وهو تعكيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command introduces another proof that the claim of other gods alongside God is false.
rows.anchor: في إظهار بطلان ذلك من جهة أخرى

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: They read the address with tā, directly addressing the polytheists; both direct address and third-person report suit a messenger relaying the command.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف بالتاء ثالث الحروف خطابا لهم

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: They read with yā here but tā in the following verse, treating the latter as God's direct act of declaring His own transcendence.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم هنا بالتاء وهناك بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf is accusative as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun: their alleged gods would be in the manner of what the polytheists say, meaning in agreement with it.
rows.anchor: والكاف في محل النصب على أنها نعت لمصدر محذوف أي كونا مشابها لما يقولون

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: The gods would seek a way to the Lord of the Throne by contesting and resisting His rule, as happens among kings; this is the argument from mutual prevention.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب سعيد ابن جبير كما أخرجه عنه ابن أبي حاتم

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Alternatively, the gods would seek nearness to God through obedience because they know His exalted rank; this resembles the verse about those invoked seeking a means to their Lord.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد وقتادة أن المعنى إذا لطلبوا الزلفى إليه تعالى والتقريب بالطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the mutual-prevention reading, the conditional is counterfactual and the argument is a hypothetical syllogism; on the nearness reading it is a condition with a categorical premise.
rows.anchor: على الأول امتناعية وعلى هذا شرطية والقياس مركب من مقدمتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi favors the mutual-prevention interpretation: the following declaration of God's purity fits an unforeseen grave consequence better than ordinary seeking of nearness, which the alleged gods would already accept.
rows.anchor: فإنه ظاهر في أن المراد بيان أنه يلزم ما يقولونه محذور عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subḥānah declares God intrinsically worthy of transcendence, far removed from the partners and daughters attributed to Him.
rows.anchor: ينزه بذاته تنزيها حقيقا به سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUluwwan is a verbal noun used without its own verb, like nabātan in the cited Quranic construction.
rows.anchor: أي تعاليا فهو مصدر من غير فعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's elevation is beyond any limit: He is at the furthest degree of existence as the necessarily existent, while partners and offspring are intrinsically impossible.
rows.anchor: بعيد الغاية بل لا غاية وراءه كيف لا وأنه تعالى في أقصى غايات الوجود

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An alternative says God is at the highest level of existence and taking offspring is among the lowest levels, as a feature of beings unable to endure.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه تعالى في أعلى مراتب الوجود وهو كونه واجب الوجود والبقاء لذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi objects that the polytheists allege partners and offspring, which are outside possibility altogether; calling these the lowest level of existence only applies relative to beings capable of them.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن ما يقولونه ليس مجرد اتخاذ الولد بل مع ما سمعت ولا ريب في أن ذلك ليس بداخل في حد الإمكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed answer that this is a comparison from lower to higher remains unconvincing; mentioning elevation after naming the Lord of the Throne is especially eloquent.
rows.anchor: واعتذر بأنه من باب التنبيه بحال الأدنى على حال الأعلى ولا يخفى أن ذكر العلو بعد عنوانه بذي العرش

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والأخوان وحفص
rows.claim: They read tasbiḥ with the feminine verb form; the other readers use the masculine form because the subject's grammatical femininity is nonliteral and separated from the verb.
rows.anchor: بالفوقانية وهي قراءة أبي عمرو والأخوين وحفص

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: They read the verb in the masculine form because the feminine subject is nonliteral and separated from the verb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون بالتحتانية لأن تأنيث الفاعل مجازي مع الفصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A past-tense reading, sabbaḥat, is also transmitted.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( سبحت ) ( له السموات السبع والأرض ومن فيهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven heavens, earth, and all within them include angels and humans and jinn; every kind of thing, animate, plant, or mineral, glorifies God.
rows.anchor: أي من الملائكة والثقلين ( وإن من شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The primary interpretation takes glorification as the testimony of created possibility and origination: each thing demonstrates God's necessary existence, unity, power, and freedom from contingent properties.
rows.anchor: والمراد من التسبيح الدلالة بلسان الحال أي تدل بإمكانها وحدوثها دلالة واضحة على وجوب وجوده تعالى ووحدته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is a transferred metaphor, as when one says that a state speaks; a representational metaphor is also possible.
rows.anchor: ففي الكلام استعارة تبعية كما في نطقت الحال وجوز أن يعتبر فيه استعارة تمثيلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The failure to understand applies to the polytheists and disbelievers just described, not humanity universally; the passage follows their false attributions with all creation's testimony against them.
rows.anchor: لما أن الخطاب للمشركين والكفرة لا للناس على العموم لأنه تقدم ذكر قبائحهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing description means God is forbearing, delaying punishment for their failure to reason correctly, and forgives those who repent and reflect.
rows.anchor: أي إنه سبحانه حليم ولذلك لم يعاجلكم بالعقوبة

rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munīr argues that the closing promise cannot address polytheists because God does not forgive their association; he takes the addressees as believers who fail to comprehend inanimate speech.
rows.anchor: وظن ابن المنير أن هذا التذييل يأبى كون الخطاب للمشركين قال : لأنه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects Ibn al-Munīr's reading because it breaks the passage's coherence; the closing phrase does not prevent the direct address to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وليس بسديد لخروج الكلام على ذلك من النظام ووجه التذييل ما سمعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading combines actual verbal glorification with state-based testimony, either as a general figurative usage or by combining literal and figurative senses; different creatures may use different modes.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بالتسبيح الدلالة على تنزيه الباري سبحانه عن لوازم الامكان وتوابع الحدوث مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A difficulty for the combined reading is that some verbal glorification is understood by polytheists; replies say they fail to reflect or benefit, or that failure to grasp one aspect counts as not understanding all.
rows.anchor: لأن من ذلك التسبيح ما يفقهه المشركون وغيرهم وهو التسبيح القالي

rows.speaker: بعض الظاهرية
rows.claim: Some literalists hold that every creature, including inanimate things, glorifies God with actual speech.
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض الظاهرية وارتضاه الراغب

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib endorses the literal interpretation that all things verbally glorify God.
rows.anchor: وارتضاه الراغب وقال في تفسير الخازن إنه الأصح

rows.speaker: الخازن
rows.claim: Al-Khāzin calls the universal, literal verbal interpretation the soundest view.
rows.anchor: وقال في تفسير الخازن إنه الأصح على أن التسبيح على معناه الحقيقي

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam objects that literal verbal glorification requires knowledge, which inanimate things lack because they lack life; otherwise the condition for knowledge would collapse.
rows.anchor: لأن هذا التسبيح لا يحصل إلا مع العلم وهو مما يتصور في الجماد لفقد شرطه العقلي وهو الحياة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: He also argues that the closing rebuke makes ignorance of verbal praise culpable, whereas failing to understand inanimate speech would not be a sin; ignorance of their testimony through signs is culpable.
rows.anchor: وأيضا التذييل السابق يأبى ذلك لدلالته على أن عدم فقه التسبيح المذكور جرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports and traditions strongly attest to audible praise; one sound report describes pebbles glorifying in the Prophet's hand.
rows.anchor: ومن تتبع الأحاديث والآثار رأي فيها ما يشهد بما ذهب إليه هذا البعض شهادة لا تكاد تقبل التأويل

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet said a dish of thريد was glorifying; several companions heard it, and the Prophet had the dish passed among them.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو الشيخ عن أنس قال : أتى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بطعام ثريد

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says the Companions counted signs as blessings; while water flowed between the Prophet's fingers, they heard its sound and glorification as they drank.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود قال : كنا أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم نعد الآيات بركة

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet's account that Noah, at death, urged his sons to say Subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi, the prayer of everything and means by which everything receives provision.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : إنا نوحا عليه السلام لما حضرته الوفاة

rows.speaker: معاذ بن أنس
rows.claim: Muʿādh ibn Anas reports the Prophet forbidding people to burden mounts as seats for roadside and market conversations; a mount may remember God more than its rider.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أحمد عن معاذ بن أنس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه مر على قوم وهم وقوفا على دواب لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet's prohibition on killing frogs, saying their croaking is glorification.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر قال : نهى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن قتل الضفدع وقال نقيقها تسبيح

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that an angel taught David to hear a frog praising God in words David had not used; David vowed to praise God with that praise.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك قال : ظن داود عليه السلام في نفسه

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: In a long report from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, David hears that seventy thousand frogs stand on one leg glorifying God, correcting his thought that no one else praised God at that hour.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أحمد في الزهد وأبو الشيخ عن شهر بن حوسب من حديث طويل أن داود علي السلام أتى البحر

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports from the Prophet that birds glorify their Lord each morning and ask Him for that day's provision.
rows.anchor: عن أبي ضمرة قال : كنا عند علي بن الحسين رضي الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A report through al-Zuhrī from Abū Bakr says that game hunted, trees cut, and branches severed are due to the scarcity of glorification.
rows.anchor: وأخرجوأخرج ابن راهوية في مسنده من طريق الزهري

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء وابن مسعود
rows.claim: A marfūʿ report from Abū al-Dardāʾ and Ibn Masʿūd gives the same account that hunting and cutting vegetation result from deficient glorification.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن الشيخ عن أبي الدرداء وابن مردوية عن ابن مسعود مثل ذلك مرفوعا أيضا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says that without the veil hiding the glorification of what is in people's homes, they could not live together.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو الشيخ عن الحسن لولا ما غم عليكم من تسبيح ما معكم من البيوت ما تقاررتم

rows.speaker: لوط بن أبي لوط
rows.claim: A report ascribed to Luṭ ibn Abī Luṭ assigns a distinct formula of glorification to each of the seven heavens.
rows.anchor: عن أبي حاتم عن لوط بن أبي لوط قال : بلغني أن تسبيح سماء الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taken together, these reports support actual verbal glorification; this is also the Sufi position, whose spiritual wayfarers may hear things praising God in diverse tongues.
rows.anchor: وهي بمجموعها متعاضدة في الدلالة على أن التسبيح قالي كما لا يخفى وهو مذهب الصوفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some early Muslims reportedly heard certain inanimate objects glorifying God.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن بعض السلف سماعا لتسبيح بعض الجمادات

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says all things glorify without restriction; another gives conditions under which dust, beads, leaves, garments, beasts, and birds cease glorifying.
rows.anchor: واختلف القائلون بهذا التسبيح فقال بعضهم : بثبوته للأشياء مطلقا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: When someone said a table was glorifying, al-Ḥasan replied that only things remaining in their original state do so.
rows.anchor: عن ابن شوذب قال : جلس الحسن مع أصحابه على مائدة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says every thing still in its original state and not dead glorifies God; death may mean departure from that original state.
rows.anchor: عن السدي أنه قال : ما من شيء على أصله الأول لم يمت

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda limits glorification to things with a spirit, such as trees and animals; treating trees as living follows ordinary language about a dried tree dying.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة أنه قال في الآية : كل شيء فيه الروح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās excludes donkeys and dogs from the universal glorification.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال كل شيء يسبح إلا الحمار والكلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi sees no basis for excluding those animals, doubts the report's attribution to Ibn ʿAbbās, and finds no reason to prefer its restriction over the many unqualified reports.
rows.anchor: ولا أرى لاستثناء ما ذكر وجها وفي القلب من صحة الرواية عن الحبر شيء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: To answer the objection that verbal praise requires awareness, some posit a fitting kind of life and knowledge in every thing, whose reality only God knows.
rows.anchor: وتقصى بعضهم عن هذا بالتزام أن لكل شيء حياة وعلما لائقين به

rows.speaker: الخواص
rows.claim: Al-Khawwāṣ, as quoted by al-Shaʿrānī, says every inanimate thing understands speech and feels pain as an animal does.
rows.anchor: عن الخواص أنه قال : كل جماد يفهم الخطاب ويتألم

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: The Greatest Shaykh says minerals and plants possess spirits normally hidden from perception; all things are living, speaking, and glorifying, though their forms differ by temperament.
rows.anchor: وقال الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره : أن المسمى بالجماد والنبات له عندنا أرواح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that an announcer's voice is witnessed by every wet and dry thing, together with prophetic law and revelation, supports this account of creaturely awareness.
rows.anchor: وقد رود أن المؤذن يشهد له مدى صوته من رطب ويابس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report about the Prophet's prayer for fever addresses it as a conscious being and directs it to leave for someone who alleges other gods.
rows.anchor: واستدل بعضهم في هذا المقام بما روي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال في دعائه للحمى

rows.speaker: السجاد
rows.claim: The al-Ṣaḥīfa contains an address to the moon that appears to ascribe awareness to it; reports also describe ʿUmar writing to the Nile and speaking to the earth during an earthquake.
rows.anchor: وجاء عن السجاد رضي الله تعالى عنه في الصحيفة في مخاطبة القمر ما هو ظاهر في أنه له شعورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no need to allegorize such reports: no one claims inanimate awareness resembles ordinary animal perception, and believers should trust truthful reports while recognizing their own limited knowledge.
rows.anchor: لا أحد يقول : إن شعور الجمادات كشعور الحيوانات الظاهرة بحيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the universal-life interpretation, the pronoun in tasbīḥahum needs no special explanation; another proposal attaches the closing statement to God's transcendence, but that move is weak.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا الذي ذكروه لا تحتاج إعادة ضمير ذوي العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi's preferred reconciliation allows both state-based and verbal glorification in every thing, with the rebuke about failure to understand directed to deficient grasp of state-based testimony.
rows.anchor: ولعل الأولى فيه أن يلتزم حمل التسبيح على ما هو الأعم من الحالي والقالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since some beings attributed glorification are deniers or silent, a figurative reading is required; the response is that context implicitly excludes them, despite an extravagant claim that even deniers sanctify God.
rows.anchor: ويشكل أيضا أن من أفراد من نسب إليه التسبيح الجحد فضلا عن الساكت فالحمل على المجاز واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A passive intensive reading, lā yufqahū, is also transmitted.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( لا يفقهون ) على صيغة المبني للمفعول من باب التفعيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Prophet recites the Quran that proclaims God's transcendence and calls people to obey it, God places a veil between him and those who deny the afterlife.
rows.anchor: الناطق بالتسبيح والتزيه ودعوتهم إلى العمل بما فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative description condemns the polytheists and recalls their disbelief in origin and return; singling out disbelief in the afterlife may prepare for the coming denial of resurrection.
rows.anchor: وأوثر الموصول على الضمير ذما لهم بما في حين الصلة ويتم به مع ما سبق الإشارة إلى كفرهم بالمبدأ والمعاد

rows.speaker: صاحب إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: The cited commentary says denial of the afterlife is singled out because it is the greatest Quranic obligation and prepares for their later rejection of resurrection.
rows.anchor: وفي إرشاد العقل السليم إنما خص بالذكر كفرهم بالآخرة من بين سائر ما كفروا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi doubts that belief in the afterlife outranks monotheism and prefers to say the mention simply prepares for the following material.
rows.anchor: فالأولى الاقتصار على أنه للتمهيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The veil prevents them from recognizing the Prophet's prophethood and high rank, which explains their brazen accusation that he is bewitched.
rows.anchor: يحجبهم من أن يدركوك على ما أنت عليه من النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mastūran may mean possessing a covering, a relational adjective; alternatively the attribution is figurative, or mafʿūl may mean fāʿil, or the veil is hidden, layered, unknown as a veil, or something by which the Messenger is covered.
rows.anchor: أي ذا ستر فهو للنسب كرجل مرطوب ومكان مهول وجارية مغنوجة

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash allows mastūr to mean sāṭir, as in māʾ dāfiq, or to be literal because the barrier is immaterial and hidden from sense perception.
rows.anchor: وفي الأخفش أن مفعول يرد بمعنى مفعول كماء دافق فمستور بمعنى ساتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akinna are many coverings over their hearts; an yafqahū may express aversion to discovering the Quran's reality, or be the object of an implied preventing verb rather than a direct complement of jaʿalnā.
rows.anchor: أغطية جمع كنان والمراد بمعونة المقام التكثير أي أكنة كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waqr is heavy deafness that blocks proper hearing, though they did hear the recitation without reflection.
rows.anchor: صمما وثقلا عظيما مانعا من سماعه اللائق به فإنهم كانوا يسمعونه من غير تدبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are figures for deep ignorance of the Prophet and strong aversion to understanding the Quran; its clear testimony makes their state worse than the earlier failure to grasp creation's signs.
rows.anchor: هذه كما قال بعض المحققين تمثيلات معربة عن كمال جهلهم بشؤن النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This figurative reading suits the earlier interpretation of glorification as testimony through created states, but not a reading where all things glorify verbally.
rows.anchor: وحمل الآية على ما ذكر من لم يجعل التسبيح فيما سبق لفظيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets the hidden veil as coverings on their hearts that prevent understanding and benefiting from the Quran; al-Zajjāj agrees.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة أنه قال : الحجاب المستور أكنة على قلوبهم أن يفقهوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi objects that this reading does not fit the barrier between the Prophet and the disbelievers without supplying two omitted terms, and duplicates the next verse without new information.
rows.anchor: إلا بتقدير مضافين أي جعلنا بين فهم قراءتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its defenders answer that the veil is a parable for being unable to hear truth, while the next verse explicitly states the implication already conveyed by denying comprehension of signs.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن الظاهر أنه لا يقدر فيه وإنما يلزم لو كان حقيقة وهذا تمثيل لهم

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says the veil prevents them from reaching and harming the Prophet when he recites; Alusi finds this plausible but weaker than the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: وعن الجبائي أن المراد بالحجاب ما يحجبهم عن إيذاء الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi ranks the protection-from-harm interpretation below the primary account after considering its context.
rows.anchor: وهو عندي مما لا بأس به وإن ذكره في معرض التفصي عن استدلال أصحابنا

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت أبي بكر
rows.claim: Asmāʾ reports that Abū Lahab's wife approached insulting the Prophet with a stone; he said she would not see him, recited Quran, and she stood by Abū Bakr without seeing him.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج أبو يعلى وابن أبي حاتم والحاكم وصححه وابن مردويه والبيهقي معافى الدلائل عن أسماء بنت أبي بكر

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت أبي بكر
rows.claim: In another version, Abū Bakr says she did not see the Prophet; the Prophet attributes this to Gabriel standing between them.
rows.anchor: وجاء في رواية أنها حين ولت ذاهبة قال أبو بكر : يا رسول الله إنها لم ترك

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam says the Prophet recited three verses before Quran recitation—one each from al-Kahf, al-Naḥl, and al-Jāthiyah—and God hid him from the polytheists through their blessing.
rows.anchor: وذكر الإمام أنه كان صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا أراد تلاوة القرءان تلا قبلها ثلاث ءايات

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The theologians argue that sight may fail despite a sound faculty and present object if God creates an impediment in the eye; they apply this to the Prophet present but unseen by the pagans.
rows.anchor: واحتج أصحابنا بذلك على أنه يجوز أن تكون الحاسة سليمة ويكون المرئي حاضرا مع أنه لا يرى

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some critical scholars say the Asmāʾ report does not fit the passage's order if its veil means an optical barrier; this also challenges the Imam's argument.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المحققين : إن حمل الحجاب على ما روي من حديث أسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports that Gabriel or another angel physically screened the Prophet indicate the obstacle was not in the pagans' eyes, though such concealment is also extraordinary; Asmāʾ's report does not explicitly identify the Quranic veil as visual.
rows.anchor: فإن كلا الخبرين ظاهر في أن المانع لم يكن في عيونهم بل هو إما جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The visual-barrier interpretation relies on accepting al-Ḥākim's authentication or another hadith scholar's endorsement; without that, the issue is less significant.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول إنما يحتاج إليه أن اعتبر تصحيح الحاكم أو نص على صحته

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats the veil and coverings as the disbelievers' own claim that their hearts and ears reject the Quran.
rows.anchor: ما تقدم حكاية لما قالوا ( قلوبنا ) في أكنة مما تدعونا إليه

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: The cited Shaykh rejects that reading: they described the Quran and Prophet as inherently unworthy of belief, not an external barrier preventing perception.
rows.anchor: ولم يرتضه شيخ الإسلام لأن قصدهم بذلك إنما هو الاخبار بما اعتقدوه في حق القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says the Zamakhsharī reading may fit a passage listing their faults, but its selection carries a Muʿtazilite doctrinal motive.
rows.anchor: نعم اختيار الزمخشري هذا الوجه مما لا يخلو عن دسيسه اعتزالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning God alone means not pairing His name with their alleged gods, as in their invocation of Allah together with al-Lāt.
rows.anchor: أي غير مقرون بذكره ذكر شيء من آلهتهم التي يزعمونها كما كانوا يقولون بالله تعالى واللات مثلا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī analyzes waḥdahu as an accusative verbal noun standing in for a circumstantial expression, with several possible derivations.
rows.anchor: الزمخشري مصدر الثلاثي يقل وحده يحده وحدا وحدة كوعده يعده وعدا وعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The state phrase may attach to the one who remembers, meaning they remember God as one, or to the remembrance, meaning they mention only Him.
rows.anchor: أي وإذا ذكرت ربك موحدا له أو موحدا بالذكر

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus parses waḥdahu as an adverb; when it follows both subject and object, it can be circumstantial of either.
rows.anchor: ومذهب يونس أنه منصوب على الظرفية وتحقيق الأقوال فيه في الرفدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wal-lawlā ad-bārihim means they fled; nufūran may be an emphatic cognate accusative, a purpose, or a circumstantial plural meaning fleeing.
rows.anchor: فهو مفعول مطلق منصوب بولوا لتقارب معناهما وجوز أن يكون مفعولا لأجله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās appears to assign the pronoun to devils, but Alusi says that attribution is scarcely sound unless reinterpreted.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وغيره عن ابن عباس ما ظاهره أنه للشياطين ولا يكاد يصح عن الحبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what they listen to while engaged in idle talk, ridicule, and mockery of the Prophet and Quran.
rows.anchor: أي متلبسين به من اللغو والاستخفاف والهزء بك وبالقرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes two men of ʿAbd al-Dār on each side of the Prophet clapping, whistling, and mixing poetry into his recitation.
rows.anchor: يروى أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام كان يقوم عن يمينه رجلان من عبد الدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi may mean what they listen amid, because of, or for; treating it as literally referring to listening with the heart or outer ears is unlikely.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون الباء للسببية أو بمعنى اللام أي نحن أعلم بما يستمعون بسببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The time clauses reinforce the warning: God knows their conduct exactly as they listen and exactly as they confer; an alternative attaches them directly to listening and conferring.
rows.anchor: فائدته كما قال شيخ الإسلام تأكيد الوعيد بالإخبار بأنه كما يقع الاستماع المزبور منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najwā may be an abstract predicate like saying Zayd is justice, or a plural meaning private interlocutors.
rows.anchor: مصدر مرفوع على الخبرية وفي ذلك ما في زيد عدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about wrongdoers explains their whispering; naming them instead of using a pronoun marks their secret counsel as an act of injustice.
rows.anchor: بدل من إذ الثانية وبيان لما يتناجون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their accusation means people would follow no one but a bewitched man, either rendered insane by sorcery or supposedly using magic to produce his claims.
rows.anchor: أي ما تتبعون إن وجد منكم الاتباع فرضا وجوز أن يكون المعنى ما تتبعون باللغو والهزء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbaydah takes masḥūr as a human possessing a sahr, or lung, and cites poetry where being fed is expressed as being enchanted; they mean the Prophet is merely human.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي عبيدة أن مسحورا بمعنى جعل له سحرا وإذا سحر أي رئة

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutaybah calls Abū ʿUbaydah's explanation forced because earlier authorities gave clearer interpretations.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتيبة : لا أدري ما الذي حمل أبا عبيدة على هذا التفسير المستكره

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says interpreting the phrase as likening the Prophet does not suit the wording that they struck examples for him.
rows.anchor: إنه لا يناسب قوله تعالى : ( أنظر كيف ضربوا لك الأمثال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They portray him variously as poet or madman despite knowing better; in all these arguments they depart from sound reasoning.
rows.anchor: أي مثلوك فقالوا تارة شاعر وتارة مجنون مع علمهم بخلافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They cannot find a viable path to an objection anyone would accept, or a path to truth; the verse threatens them and consoles the Prophet.
rows.anchor: طريقا ما إلى طعن يمكن أن يقبله أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resurrection denial is coordinated with their striking examples; it is another astonishing expression of their mockery.
rows.anchor: ولما عجب من ضربهم الأمثال عطف عليه أمرا آخر يعجب منه أيضا

rows.speaker: في الكشف
rows.claim: The more coherent reading takes this resurrection question through the following statements as explanation of their striking examples, rather than saying they literally likened the Prophet.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أن يكون هذا إلى تمام المقالات الثلاث تفسيرا لضربوا لك الأمثال

rows.speaker: في الكشف
rows.claim: On that reading, they mock the Prophet and Quran, then mock resurrection, which is even more astonishing because reason points to it at least in general.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر استهزاءهم به صلى الله عليه وسلم وبالقرآن عجبه من استهزائهم بمضمونه من البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says coordinating the statement with their going astray is awkward, while the explanatory coordination with striking examples needs no forced ellipsis and fits better.
rows.anchor: مما لا يحسن لعدم ظهور دخوله معه في حيز الفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also sees no obstacle to linking their public resurrection question with the wrongdoers' whispered accusation; public utterance and differing verb tense do not preclude it.
rows.anchor: هل ثم مانع من عطف ( قالوا ) على ( يقول الظالمون ) وجعل هذا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rufāt means what has been crushed and broken; the pattern faʿāl commonly names things pulverized or scattered.
rows.anchor: والرفات ما تكسر وبلى من كل شيء وكثر بناء فعال في كل ما تحطم وتفرق

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains rufāt as dust, an interpretation also attributed to al-Farrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وغيره عن مجاهد أنه التراب وهو قول الفراء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains rufāt as dust.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر وغيره عن ابن عباس أنه الغبار

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad defines rufāt as anything pulverized extremely finely; the reported definitions are close.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد : هو كل شيء مدقوق مبالغ في دقه وهي أقوال متقاربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative is emphatic denial: they deem resurrection impossible because living softness and cohesion conflict with the dry remains that disperse.
rows.anchor: والهمزة للاستفهام الانكاري مفيدة لكمال الاستبعاد والاستنكار للبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh is temporal, governed by the implied resurrection question rather than the noun itself because inna and the interrogative occupy clause-initial position; setting the question at that state sharpens denial.
rows.anchor: متمحضة للظرفية والعامل فيها ما دل عليه قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional parsing with an omitted answer is possible but uncommon; the denial concerns being raised after that state, not their being actually resurrected while bones and dust.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تكون شرطية وجوابها مقدر أي نبعث أو نحوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic inna and lām intensify their denial; new creation is either an absolute object for being resurrected or a circumstantial description of the created beings.
rows.anchor: وتحلية الجملة بأن واللام لتأكيد الإنكار لا لإنكار التأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to become stone or iron answers the disbelievers' claim and brings the unimaginable within their own terms.
rows.anchor: جوابا لهم وتقريبا لما استبعدوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command echoes their past-tense claim and is rhetorical matching; its force is abasement and disregard.
rows.anchor: فهو من باب المشاكلة والمقابلة بالجنس

rows.speaker: صاحب الإيضاح
rows.claim: The author of al-Īḍāḥ classifies it as a command of humiliation; al-Ṭībī calls it a command of subjugation, but the latter's account is not apparent to al-Kashf.
rows.anchor: وجعله صاحب الإيضاح أمر إهانة والفاضل الطيبي أمر تسخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi considers a figurative imperative expressing humiliation the soundest interpretation; reading it as a report that they are stones does not match reality.
rows.anchor: فالصواب أنه للإهانة كما جنح إليه صاحب الإيضاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥijārah is a plural of stone; ḥadīd is a singular collective with plural forms, and the challenge means becoming members of either kind.
rows.anchor: والحجارة جمع حجر كأحجار وهو معروف وكذا الحديد وهو مفرد وجمعه حدائد وحديدات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any other creation they regard as farthest from life is left for them to imagine; God can restore them because bodies equally receive properties, and bones once possessed life.
rows.anchor: أي مخلوقا آخر ( مما يكبر في صدوركم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the immense creation they imagine is the heavens, earth, and mountains.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : الذي يكبر السموات والأرض والجبال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the greatest thing in human minds is death, so even becoming death itself would not prevent restoration.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وابن عمر والحسن وابن جبير أنهم قالوا : ما يكبر في صدورهم الموت

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar joins the view that what looms largest in human hearts is death.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وابن عمر والحسن وابن جبير أنهم قالوا : ما يكبر في صدورهم الموت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan joins the view that what looms largest in human hearts is death.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وابن عمر والحسن وابن جبير أنهم قالوا : ما يكبر في صدورهم الموت

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr joins the view that what looms largest in human hearts is death, though Alusi says this is not the phrase's apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وابن عمر والحسن وابن جبير أنهم قالوا : ما يكبر في صدورهم الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer identifies the restorer as the one who originated them the first time from earth without precedent; one capable of that can revive decayed bones.
rows.anchor: الذي فطركم ( أي القادر العظيم الذي اخترعكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause can be parsed with an omitted predicate, as subject of an omitted verb, or as predicate of an omitted subject; first time is an adverb of originating.
rows.anchor: والموصول مبتدأ خبره يعيدكم المحذوف لدلالة السؤال عليه أو فاعل به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains their head movement as mocking disbelief; Alusi cites two lines illustrating nodding the head in denial.
rows.anchor: أي سيحركونها نحوك استهزاء كما روي عن ابن عباس وأنشد عليه قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains inġāḍ as moving the head up and down; Abū al-Haytham says it is a head movement of denial.
rows.anchor: وفسر الفراء الانغاض بتحريك الرأس بارتفاع وانخفاض وقال أبو الهيثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question when resurrection will happen is mockery; its pronoun refers to the promised restoration or the resurrection implied by the discourse.
rows.anchor: متى هو ( أي ما ذكرته من الإعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may be near because its arrival is certain; its timing is unseen, known only to God, and qareeban has several plausible syntactic analyses.
rows.anchor: عسى أن يكون ( ذلك ( قريبا 15 ( فإن ما هو محقق اتيانه قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says asa already means nearness, so saying it may be near is tautological; al-Raḍī denies that nearness is asa's established meaning, preserving the expectation sense.
rows.anchor: واعترض بأن عسى للمقاربة فكأنه قيل : قرب أن يكون قريبا

rows.speaker: نجم الأئمة
rows.claim: Najm al-Aʾimma says asa does not lexically or conventionally mean nearness; the wording therefore means it is hoped or expected to be near.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن نجم الأئمة لم يثبت معنى المقاربة في عسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm may depend on an omitted remember-command, replace qareeban as a time expression, or attach to a form of be or resurrection through several debated grammatical paths.
rows.anchor: يوم يدعوكم ( منصوب بفعل مضمر أي اذكروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some additional parses depend on strained construction with an implicit source pronoun or an unconvincing genitive clause; Alusi calls that effort forced.
rows.anchor: وجعله بدلا من الضمير المستتر بدل اشتمال ولم يرفع لأنه إذا أضيف إلى مثل هذه الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling and responding are commonly figurative for resurrection and rising, as with the creative command kun fa-yakūn; the figure conveys speed and ease.
rows.anchor: والدعاء قيل : مجاز عن البعث وكذا الاستجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gathering is for judgment, since the afterlife has no further legal obligations and a master's summons is to use or question a servant.
rows.anchor: وعلى أن المقصود الاحضار للحساب والجزاء فإن دعوة السيد لعبده

rows.speaker: الإمام وأبو حيان
rows.claim: The Imam and Abū Ḥayyān take the summons as an audible call, the final trumpet blast, linked with the caller from a nearby place.
rows.anchor: وقال الإمام وأبو حيان : يدعوكم بالنداء الذي يسمعكم وهو النفخة الأخيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further account says Isrāfīl, or Gabriel in another version, calls decayed bodies from the Rock in Jerusalem to return to life.
rows.anchor: ويقال إن إسرافيل عليه السلام وفي رواية جبرائيل عليه السلام ينادي على صخرة بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abū al-Dardāʾ reports the Prophet saying people will be summoned by their own and their fathers' names, so they should choose good names; this may concern accounting after resurrection.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الدرداء أنه قال : قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إنكم تدعون يوم القيامة بأسمائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some prefer the figurative reading because a literal call would address scattered inanimate particles; those allowing literal speech say it could be a creative command addressed even to nonexistents.
rows.anchor: فقيل إن فيه إشارة إلى امتناع الحمل على الحقيقة لما يلزم من الحمل عليها خطاب الجماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that a permissible literal reading must make the trope metonymy rather than metaphor is, Alusi says, an easy matter.
rows.anchor: وأما إنه لو لم تمتنع إرادة الحقيقة لكان كناية لا مجاز فأمر سهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial bi-ḥamdihi refers to the disbelievers: they answer while praising God's power or acknowledging that all praise belongs to Him for blessings, since knowledge then is necessary.
rows.anchor: حال من ضمير المخاطبين وهم الكفار كما هو الظاهر والباء للملابسة

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr says people leave their graves saying, 'Glory to You, God, and praise be to You'; even disbelievers may say this then without benefit.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جرير أنه قال : يخرجون من قبورهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats praise as figurative: they submit to resurrection so thoroughly that their forced compliance resembles a willing, grateful acceptance.
rows.anchor: وحمل الزمخشري ذلك على المجاز والمراد المغالبة في انقيادهم للبعث

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī treats bi-ḥamdihi as parenthetical between coordinated clauses: the Prophet's report will prove true when the summons comes, praise be to God.
rows.anchor: وعن الطبري أن ( بحمده ) معترض بين متعاطفين اعتراضه بين اسم إن وخبرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects al-Ṭabarī's parenthetical interpretation as strained and not readily recoverable from the words.
rows.anchor: وملخصه يكون ذلك على اختلاف اعتقادكم والحمد لله تعالى ولا يخفى أنه معنى متكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view shifts the addressees at qareeban from disbelievers to believers, who answer with praise for God's favor and guidance to faith.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخطاب للمؤمنين وانقطع خطاب الكافرين عند قوله تعالى : ( قريبا

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that those who profess God's oneness have no fear in their graves or at resurrection and emerge praising God for removing sorrow.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمرقال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas transmits a parallel report that believers in God's oneness have no fear at death, in their graves, or at gathering.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية عن أنس مرفوعا ليس على أهل لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr offers a third view: both believers and disbelievers say the reported words.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الخطاب للفريقين وكلهم يقولون : ما روي عن ابن جبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tazunnūn coordinates with تستجيبون, or may have an implied subject as a circumstantial clause; their brief stay may refer to the graves or worldly life.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه عطف على ( تستجيبون ) وإليه ذهب الحوفي وغيره

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن عباس
rows.claim: Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās say they will regard the interval between the two blasts as short because punishment is lifted then, and they ask who roused them from their resting place.
rows.anchor: كما روى غير واحد عن قتادة وعن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما يستقلون لبثهم بين النفختين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking the brief duration as time spent on the plain of resurrection is far-fetched because their ultimate destination is Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل يستقلون لبثهم في عرصة القيامة لما أن عاقبة أمرهم الدخول إلى النار وهذا في غاية البعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓann may mean ordinary conjecture or certainty; the negative inna-clause suspends its verb, and qaleelan qualifies an omitted time or duration.
rows.anchor: والظن يحتمل أن يكون على بابه ويحتمل أن يكون بمعنى اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servants are believers, honored by the possessive attribution; in exchanges with polytheists they should use the best words and avoid harshness, as in the cited instruction to dispute graciously.
rows.anchor: أي المؤمنين فالإضافة لتشريف المضاف ( يقولوا ( عند محاورتهم

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes sayū as the response to an omitted command quoted after 'tell My servants,' with a deleted saying clause.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب الأخفش ولكون المقول لهم هم المؤمنون

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj treats sayū as the quoted command itself, with a deleted imperative lām governing its jussive form.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : إن يقولوا هو المقول وجزمه بلام الأمر محذوفة

rows.speaker: المازني
rows.claim: Al-Māzinī also takes it as the quoted command but parses the present verb as imperative-like through substitution; Alusi finds this unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: وقال المازني : إنه المقول أيضا إلا أنه مضارع مبني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command prevents Satan from stirring conflict between believers and polytheists through harsh speech, which would harden hostility and prolong corruption.
rows.anchor: أي يفسد ويهيج الشر بين المؤمنين والمشركين بالمخاشنة

rows.speaker: طلحة
rows.claim: Ṭalḥah reads yanziġ with a kasra on zāy; Abū Ḥātim suggests it may be dialect, while the standard reading has fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة ( ينزغ ) بكسر الزاي قال أبو حاتم : لعلها لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan is an evident and longstanding enemy; mubīnan derives from intransitive abāna, meaning manifest.
rows.anchor: ظاهر العداوة فهو من أبان اللازم والجملة تعليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best words include telling them that God knows them and may guide them to faith or let them die in disbelief; do not declare them destined for Hell, since their end is unknown.
rows.anchor: وإن يشأ يعذبكم ( بالإماتة على الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These clauses interrupt the instruction as an example of gracious speech to the polytheists and counsel against provoking them.
rows.anchor: وهذا تفسير التي هي أحسن والجملتان اعتراض بينهما والخطاب فيه للمشركين

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī reads aw as a break or redirection rather than true alternatives; Ibn al-Anbārī calls it permissive breadth in God's options, an analysis Alusi finds excessive.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني : هي للإضراب ولذا كررت معها أن

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī calls aw permissive, as in 'sit with al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn,' meaning both options are available; Alusi rejects the explanation as overextended.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري : دخلت أو هنا لسعة الأمرين عند الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is not entrusted to force them into Islam; he was sent as bearer of glad tidings and warning, so he and his companions should show patience and gentleness before the sword verse.
rows.anchor: أي موكولا ومفوضا إليك أمرهم تقسرهم على الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the outward and inward states of all in heaven and earth and selects for prophethood and authority whom His wisdom deems worthy.
rows.anchor: وبأحوالهم الظاهرة والباطنة فيختار منهم لنبوته وولايته من يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This answers the objection that an orphan from Abū Ṭālib could not be a prophet or that poor followers such as Ṣuhayb, Bilāl, and Khabbāb should not accompany him instead of elites.
rows.anchor: وهو رد عليه إذ قالوا : بعيد أن يكون يتيم ابن أبي طالب نبيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning heaven rebuts their demand for angels, and mentioning earth rebuts their demand that revelation descend on a notable man from the two towns.
rows.anchor: وذكر من في السموات لإبطال قولهم ( لولا أنزل علينا الملائكة ) وذكر من في الأرض

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī attaches the phrase about heaven and earth to an omitted word for knowledge, fearing that attaching it to aʿlam would imply God does not know other matters.
rows.anchor: فما قاله أبو علي من أن الجار متعلق بعلم محذوفا ولا يجوز تعلقه بأعلم

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān objects that ʿalima does not govern bi in this usage, but takes a direct object.
rows.anchor: على أن أبا حيان أنكر تعدي علم بالباء وإنما يتعدى لواحد بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says the preceding explanation answers Abū ʿAlī's objection; specifying these inhabitants does not restrict God's comprehensive knowledge.
rows.anchor: ناشيء عن عدم العلم بما ذكرنا على أن أبا حيان أنكر تعدي علم بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets are favored through inward virtues, sacred qualities, and revealed scriptures, not through wealth or followers.
rows.anchor: بالفضائل النفسانية والمزايا القدسية وإنزال الكتب السماوية لا بكثرة الأموال والأتباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David's example shows that his distinction was receiving the Zabūr, not kingship or sovereignty.
rows.anchor: بيان لحيثية تفضيله عليه الصلاة والسلام وأنه بإيتائه الزبور لا بإيتائه الملك والسلطنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse hints at Muhammad's superiority as final prophet and leader of the best community; the Zabūr promised that God's righteous servants would inherit the earth.
rows.anchor: وفيه إيذان بتفضيل نبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم فإن كونه عليه الصلاة والسلام خاتم الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some call the reference to the Zabūr an allusion, illustrated by a story of a poet reminding the caliph al-Manṣūr of a promise through a familiar verse.
rows.anchor: ونص بعضهم أن هذا من باب التلميح نحو قصة المنصور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zabūr may be a passive participle or verbal noun; under Ḥamzah's vocalization some parse it as a plural of zubr, 'written texts,' used as the book's title.
rows.anchor: والزبور في الأصل وصف المفعول كالحلوب أو مصدر كالقبول

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas says the Zabūr consists of praise of God, prayer, and glorification.
rows.anchor: عن الربيع بن أنس قال : الزبور ثناء على الله عز وجل ودعاء وتسبيح

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the Zabūr was a prayer taught to David, with praise and exaltation of God but no lawful or forbidden rules, duties, or penalties.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة قال : كنا نحدث أن الزبور دعاء علمه داود
